B. Covered Aircraft Requirements (§§ 61.113(i)(1) and 91.319(j))
In section 2307(j) of FESSA, as promulgated in 2016, a covered aircraft was defined as an aircraft that (1) is authorized under Federal law to carry not more than 6 occupants; and (2) has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 6,000 pounds. These requirements were implemented for aircraft authorized under Federal law.[12]
Section 828(a)(4) of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 amended section 2307(j) of FESSA to increase the number of occupants an aircraft is authorized to carry under Federal law from 6 to 7 and to increase the maximum certificated takeoff weight from not more than 6,000 pounds to not more than 12,500 pounds. Additionally, section 828(a)(4) added a third provision to section 2307(j) of FESSA to exclude transport category rotorcraft certificated to airworthiness standards under part 29. To note, these amendments were immediately adopted within 49 U.S.C. 44703 note (FESSA).
For aircraft authorized under Federal law, this final rule revises § 61.113(i)(1) to reflect the provisions of section 2307(j), as amended by section 828(a)(4).[13]

3.1 What Do I Need to Fly Under BasicMed?
1. Hold a current and valid U.S. driver’s license.
2. Hold or have held a medical certificate issued by the FAA at any point after
July 14, 2006.
3. Answer the health questions on the Comprehensive Medical Examination
Checklist (CMEC).
4. Get your physical examination by any State-licensed physician, and have that
physician complete the CMEC (be sure to keep the CMEC).
5. Take the BasicMed online medical education course. Keep the course
completion document issued to you by the course provider.
3.2 What Are My BasicMed Privileges? You can conduct any operation that you would
otherwise be able to conduct using your pilot certificate and a third-class medical
certificate, except you are limited to:
1. Fly with no more than five passengers.
2. Fly an aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of no more than
6,000 lbs.
3. Fly an aircraft that is authorized to carry no more than 6 occupants.
4. Flights within the United States, at an indicated airspeed of 250 knots or less,
and at an altitude at or below 18,000 feet mean sea level (MSL).
5. You may not fly for compensation or hire.

FAA Updates BasicMed Program
Friday, November 15, 2024
WASHINGTON – The Federal Aviation Administration updated its BasicMed regulations to allow pilots to operate larger aircraft and carry more passengers.
BasicMed, which took effect in 2017, allows pilots to fly without holding an FAA medical certificate provided they meet certain conditions.
The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 required the FAA to expand BasicMed to:
Increase the number of allowable passengers to six from five, and the number of occupants to seven from six.
Increase the maximum aircraft takeoff weight to 12,500 lbs. from 6,000 lbs., excluding transport category helicopters.
Allow pilot examiners to conduct flight checks using BasicMed in aircraft that are covered by the BasicMed rule. Information for examiners is available here.

verdict.summary:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — FAA BasicMed aircraft limits (United States), current form

SCOPE AND VERSION CONTROL
Jurisdiction: United States, FAA. Regime: BasicMed, i.e. 14 CFR 61.113(i) operating under the medical relief of 14 CFR part 68 and section 2307 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 (FESSA), 49 U.S.C. 44703 note, as amended by section 828 of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024. The version stated here is the post-amendment text as it currently appears in eCFR § 61.113(i)(1) (amendment line 'Amdt. 61-158, 89 FR 90577, Nov. 18, 2024') and as restated in the FAA final rule published at 89 FR (FR Doc. 2024-26935, Nov. 18, 2024). If a precise effective date is needed for a legal filing, confirm it against the effective-date line in the FR document header; the operative numbers below are those in the current codified text.

CONTROLLING TEXT (verbatim, 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1))
"The aircraft is authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, is operated with no more than 6 passengers on board, and is not a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under part 29 of this chapter."

1. ANSWER TABLE (operative limits)
| Limit | Value | Rule text |
|---|---|---|
| Maximum takeoff weight | 12,500 lb (maximum takeoff / maximum certificated takeoff weight) | 61.113(i)(1) |
| Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry | 7 occupants, inclusive of required flight crew | 61.113(i)(1); 91.319(j) for experimental |
| Passengers on board | 6 passengers | 61.113(i)(1) |
| Additional exclusion | Not a transport category rotorcraft certificated under part 29 | 61.113(i)(1) |

All three are ceilings ('not more than' = ≤). The boundary values themselves comply: an aircraft at exactly 12,500 lb MTOW, authorized for exactly 7 occupants, flown with exactly 6 passengers on board, is within BasicMed.

2. DEFINITIONS THAT DECIDE COMPLIANCE
2.1 'Authorized to carry' = the aircraft's design approval, not seats installed. For type-certificated aircraft the design approval is the TC, STC, or amended TC; for experimental aircraft see 14 CFR 91.319(j) ('No person may operate an aircraft that has an experimental certificate under § 61.113(i) ... unless the aircraft is carrying not more than 7 occupants'). An airframe certificated for more occupants than the limit does not qualify merely because fewer seats are installed; conversely, an airframe whose design approval authorizes 7 or fewer occupants qualifies even if more seats are physically fitted. Determine the number from the Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS) or the applicable STC/ATC, not from the seat count or the POH seating diagram. (This principle is stated in AC 68-1A §5.1.2 and the Jul/Aug 2017 FAA Safety Briefing, e.g. PA-32/PA-34 variants; the principle survives the 2024 amendment — only the number changed from 6 to 7.)
2.2 'Occupants' includes the pilot flying under BasicMed and any required flightcrew members. Passengers = persons on board other than required flightcrew. A pilot aboard who is not a required flightcrew member and is not a flight instructor giving instruction counts as a passenger (AC 68-1A §5.2.2.1).
2.3 Reconciliation of the two numbers (must not be conflated): the 7-occupant limit is a property of the aircraft's authorization; the 6-passenger limit is a property of the flight. Because occupants = required crew + passengers, the passenger allowance is effectively min(6, 7 − required crew):
- Aircraft requiring 1 pilot: 6 passengers + 1 pilot = 7 occupants → at both limits simultaneously. Compliant.
- Aircraft requiring 2 pilots: 7 − 2 = 5 passengers maximum. Carrying 6 passengers would put 8 occupants on board, breaching the 7-occupant ceiling. So on a two-crew aircraft the occupant limit binds, and 5 (not 6) is the operative passenger number.
- Ferry/instruction case with an extra required crew member: same arithmetic, 7 − required crew.
2.4 Weight: the figure is maximum takeoff weight as certificated (the statute's phrase is 'maximum certificated takeoff weight'); it is not maximum landing weight, not zero-fuel weight, and not the actual takeoff weight on a given day. An aircraft whose certificated MTOW exceeds 12,500 lb cannot be brought under BasicMed by loading light.
2.5 Transport category rotorcraft certificated to part 29 airworthiness standards are excluded outright regardless of weight or seating.

3. DETERMINATION PROCEDURE FOR A SPECIFIC AIRCRAFT (apply in order; any 'no' = not a BasicMed covered aircraft)
Step 1 — Airworthiness basis: identify the design approval (TC/STC/ATC) or experimental certificate. Record the document number.
Step 2 — Occupant authorization: read the approved occupant capacity from the TCDS/STC/ATC (or, for experimental, the operating limitations). If > 7 → fail. If ≤ 7 → pass.
Step 3 — Weight: read maximum takeoff weight from the TCDS/STC/ATC. If > 12,500 lb → fail. If ≤ 12,500 lb → pass.
Step 4 — Rotorcraft screen: if the aircraft is a transport category rotorcraft certificated under part 29 → fail.
Step 5 — Flight planning: compute required flightcrew N (1 or 2 per the approved flight manual/type design). Max passengers = min(6, 7 − N). Brief the crew that the limit applies to the whole flight, each portion of it; the pilot acting as PIC under BasicMed cannot act as PIC at any point in a flight that exceeds the limits even if another pilot with a medical certificate is aboard.
Step 6 — Retain evidence: TCDS/STC/ATC extract showing occupant capacity and MTOW, kept with the CMEC and the BasicMed course completion certificate.

4. WORKED EXAMPLES (all consistent with §1)
- Example A: Part 23 single-engine piston, MTOW 3,400 lb, certificated for 4 occupants, one required pilot, 3 passengers aboard → pass (3 ≤ 6; 4 ≤ 7; 3,400 ≤ 12,500).
- Example B: Turboprop, MTOW 10,000 lb, certificated for 9 occupants → fail on occupants (9 > 7) even if only 6 seats installed.
- Example C: Jet, MTOW 12,500 lb exactly, certificated for 7 occupants, one required pilot, 6 passengers → pass at every boundary simultaneously.
- Example D: Aircraft certificated for 8 occupants altered by STC to an approved capacity of 7 → pass, provided the STC is the basis of certification (see §2.1).
- Example E: Twin requiring two pilots, MTOW 9,000 lb, certificated for 7 occupants, 6 passengers planned → fail; max passengers = 7 − 2 = 5.
- Example F: Aircraft with certificated MTOW 12,600 lb flown at an actual takeoff weight of 11,900 lb → fail (§2.4).
- Example G: Part 29 transport category helicopter, MTOW 10,000 lb, 6 seats → fail (express exclusion).

5. SUPERSEDED VALUES — DO NOT USE (the main error source in circulation)
Before section 828 of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, the limits were 6,000 lb maximum certificated takeoff weight, 6 occupants, and 5 passengers. The 2024 amendment changed them to 12,500 lb, 7 occupants, and 6 passengers (FR Doc. 2024-26935: 'Increase the number of allowable passengers from 5 to 6 and occupants from 6 to 7'; 'Increase the maximum takeoff weight from 6,000 pounds to 12,500 pounds'). The following grounded sources still print the OLD numbers and must not be quoted as current:
- FAA AC 68-1A (dated 5/3/17): 'no more than 6,000 lbs', 'no more than 6 occupants', 'no more than five passengers'.
- FAA Safety Briefing, July/August 2017: '6,000 pounds or less ... not more than six occupants', 'Max Passengers (five)'.
A document-reviewer who quotes either of those as the answer will be wrong by 6,500 lb, one occupant, and one passenger. Note also that AC 68-1A has not been reissued in the grounded material; treat it as historical guidance on interpretation (definitions, design-approval method) but not as the source of the numbers.

6. OTHER BASICMED LIMITS (context only — outside the three asked, stated so they are not conflated with the aircraft limits)
14 CFR 61.113(i)(2): the flight, including each portion, is not carried out above 18,000 ft MSL; not outside the United States unless authorized by the country concerned; not at an indicated airspeed above 250 knots. BasicMed also excludes operations for compensation or hire (subject to the ordinary private-pilot exceptions of 61.113(b)–(e)). Pilot-side prerequisites: valid U.S. driver's license; a medical certificate held at some point after July 14, 2006, not denied/revoked/suspended/withdrawn; CMEC examination by a state-licensed physician; BasicMed online course completion; documents retained in the logbook (61.113(i)(3); part 68).

7. SOURCE REGISTER (grounded, with fetch hashes)
- 14 CFR 61.113(i) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-61/section-61.113 (fetched 2026-11-23T21:24:29Z, sha256 de6b7248669d). Primary authority for all three numbers.
- FAA final rule, FR Doc. 2024-26935 (Nov. 18, 2024) — https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/full_text/html/2024/11/18/2024-26935.html (sha256 5c7884dbe3ce). Amendment history and rationale; §91.319(j) occupant limit for experimental aircraft.
- FAA BasicMed page — https://www.faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med (sha256 6453d3e819f6). 'Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants'; 'Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds'; 'Carries not more than six passengers'.
- FAA news release, 'FAA Updates BasicMed Program' (Nov. 15, 2024) — https://www.faa.gov/newsroom/faa-updates-basicmed-program (sha256 26f9411661ea).
- AC 68-1A (sha256 73fca0dcbc98) and FAA Safety Briefing Jul/Aug 2017 (sha256 4cf7d0c950c8) — historical only; superseded figures.

8. NOTE ON THE PROOF OF ABSENCE FOR ASK 2
The harness recorded that the FAA BasicMed page's full text contains none of 'maximum takeoff weight', '6,000 pounds', '6,000 lbs', 'MTW'. That search does not establish that the page is silent on the weight limit: the page states it as 'maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds', which none of those literal strings matches. Accordingly ask 2 is not a 'page states none' case and is not listed in not_stated; it is answered as 12,500 lb, supported by that page and independently by 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1), FR Doc. 2024-26935, and the FAA news release. No figure in this memo exceeds a limit stated in this memo; the only sub-12,500 and sub-7/6 figures present are in §5, explicitly labeled superseded.

9. BOTTOM LINE
Under BasicMed in the United States a pilot may fly an aircraft that is authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants (including required flight crew), has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, is operated with not more than 6 passengers on board, and is not a part 29 transport category rotorcraft.

These Regulations amend the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (“the 2015 Regulations”) (S.I. 2015/621). These Regulations come into force on 1st April 2026.

We are alert to concerns about young people’s employment prospects
In making its recommendations for the 18-20 Year Old Rate, the Commission pays particular attention to whether increases in the youth rates have caused youth employment to fall.
While the Commission recognises that labour market outcomes for young people have deteriorated over the past two years, we are not aware of any robust evidence that higher youth rates have contributed to these falls. However, this remains an important question to ask.
Outcomes for young people are largely driven by the recent trends in the industries in which they work. Hospitality and retail are particularly important as they are the largest employers of young people. The tight labour market that followed the pandemic meant businesses (particularly in hospitality) struggled to find workers and so recruited more young people. Subsequently, labour market conditions have weakened and youth employment has fallen.

verdict.summary:
UK MINIMUM WAGE RATES EFFECTIVE FROM APRIL 2026 — FACTUAL DETERMINATION

1. ANSWERS

| # | Rate | Age band | Hourly rate from 1 April 2026 | Previous rate (to 31 March 2026) | Increase |
|---|------|----------|-------------------------------|----------------------------------|----------|
| 1 | National Living Wage (NLW) | 21 and over | £12.71 | £12.21 | +£0.50 (+4.1%) |
| 2 | National Minimum Wage (NMW), 18–20 Year Old Rate | 18 to 20 (18 or over but not yet 21) | £10.85 | £10.00 | +£0.85 (+8.5%) |

Both figures are in pounds sterling per hour, to the nearest penny, and apply UK-wide (England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland).

2. EFFECTIVE DATE

Both rates take effect on 1 April 2026. This is the commencement date stated in the amending instrument ("Coming into force 1st April 2026"; reg. 1(2)) and the date used in all GOV.UK/Low Pay Commission (LPC) publications ("rates change on 1 April every year"). Note the distinction: the UK tax year begins 6 April 2026, but the NMW/NLW uprating date is 1 April 2026, so payroll periods spanning 1–5 April 2026 must already use the new rates. The rates remain in force until 31 March 2027.

3. LEGAL AND OFFICIAL BASIS (three concordant sources)

(a) Primary instrument — The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/357, made 19 March 2026, in force 1 April 2026, extending to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Regulation 2(2) amends reg. 4 of the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (SI 2015/621): for "£12.21" substitute "£12.71". Regulation 2(3)(a) amends reg. 4A(1)(b): for "£10.00" substitute "£10.85". The Explanatory Note confirms reg. 2(2) is the NLW for workers aged 21 or over and reg. 2(3)(a) is the NMW for workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21. Signed by Kate Dearden, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Department for Business and Trade, 19 March 2026.

(b) LPC report "The National Minimum Wage in 2026" (published 1 April 2026): "From 1 April 2026, all rates of the National Minimum Wage, including the National Living Wage, increase. These increases follow recommendations made by the Low Pay Commission in October 2025." Table: National Living Wage (21 and over) £12.71 (+£0.50, 4.1%); 18-20 Year Old Rate £10.85 (+£0.85, 8.5%). Also states "The 18-20 Year Old Rate increases by 8.5 per cent in April to reach £10.85."

(c) LPC advice page "Minimum wage rates for 2026" (published 26 November 2025): "The Government has announced the 2026 increases... These will be effective from April 2026. The Government accepted in full the recommendations of the independent Low Pay Commission (LPC)." Table repeats £12.71 and £10.85.

(d) GOV.UK operational guidance page "National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage rates" — current rates table, row "April 2026": 21 and over £12.71; 18 to 20 £10.85; under 18 £8; apprentice £8. The page also states: "aged 21 to get the National Living Wage — the minimum wage will still apply for workers aged 20 and under."

Status: these are legislated, in-force rates, not projections or LPC recommendations awaiting acceptance. The Government accepted the LPC recommendations in full and the amending statutory instrument was made on 19 March 2026.

4. ADJACENT RATES FROM 1 APRIL 2026 (for completeness and to prevent mis-citation)

| Band | Rate from 1 April 2026 | Previous | Increase |
|------|------------------------|----------|----------|
| 21 and over (NLW) | £12.71 | £12.21 | +£0.50 (4.1%) |
| 18–20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 | £10.00 | +£0.85 (8.5%) |
| 16–17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 | £7.55 | +£0.45 (6.0%) |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 | £7.55 | +£0.45 (6.0%) |
| Accommodation offset (daily, not hourly) | £11.10 | £10.66 (implied by −£0.44 / 4.1%) | +£0.44 (4.1%) |

5. SCOPE, DEFINITIONS AND CAVEATS

- "National Living Wage" is the statutory rate for the 21-and-over band only (since 1 April 2024; it applied at 23+ from April 2021 and 25+ before that). The 18–20 figure is legally the National Minimum Wage 18–20 Year Old Rate; it is not a "living wage".
- The voluntary Real Living Wage (Living Wage Foundation, currently calculated on a different methodology, with separate UK and London figures) is a distinct, non-statutory rate and must not be substituted for either figure above.
- Apprentices: an apprentice aged 21 in the first year of their apprenticeship is entitled to the apprentice rate (£8.00 from 1 April 2026), not the NLW; an apprentice aged 21 who has completed the first year is entitled to £12.71.
- Forward context (not part of the answer): the same GOV.UK page lists April 2027 rates of £13.21 (21+), £11.27 (18–20), £8.31 (under 18), £8.31 (apprentice). The LPC report notes a stated Government policy intention to remove the 18–20 Year Old Rate; if that banding changes before April 2027, only forward-looking figures would need revisiting — the April 2026 answers above are unaffected.
- This is a factual lookup and written determination; no code, data change or repository artefact is involved. The deliverable is the two figures plus their legal provenance, as set out above.

6. HOW TO APPLY / VERIFY

Step 1 — Confirm the pay period start date. Any hours worked on or after 1 April 2026 are paid at the new rates; hours up to and including 31 March 2026 at the old rates (£12.21 / £10.00).
Step 2 — Confirm the worker's age in the pay reference period. 21 and over → £12.71. 18, 19 or 20 → £10.85. Under 18 → £8.00. Apprentice in first year or under 19 → £8.00.
Step 3 — Check against the statutory instrument text at legislation.gov.uk (SI 2026/357, regs. 2(2) and 2(3)(a)) if a dispute arises; the Explanatory Note is sufficient for most payroll queries.
Step 4 — Recompute: £12.21 + £0.50 = £12.71 (4.1%); £10.00 + £0.85 = £10.85 (8.5%). Both agree with the published percentage increases.
Step 5 — If quoting the rate externally, cite the source and its date (e.g. "SI 2026/357, in force 1 April 2026" or "LPC, The National Minimum Wage in 2026, published 1 April 2026").
